# Diagnosing Stuck-in-Park and Delayed Door Unlock on a 2007 Chevy Cobalt

Intermittent issues with an automatic transmission's shift interlock system often stem from electrical failures rather than mechanical binding, provided the brake lights function correctly. In your case, the loud click audible beneath the steering column when pressing the release button is a critical diagnostic clue. This sound indicates that the vehicle's Electronic Control Module (ECM) or Body Control Module (BCM) is attempting to energize the solenoid but failing to hold the circuit closed, or the mechanical plunger within the solenoid is not actuating fully despite receiving power.

The distinction between the "shift interlock solenoid" and the "shifter solenoid" is vital for troubleshooting. The shifter solenoid controls the actual hydraulic engagement of gears; failure here typically results in inability to shift into Drive or Reverse, often accompanied by distinct whining noises or harsh shifts. The shift interlock solenoid, however, is a latching solenoid located near the steering column (often accessible under the dashboard near the kick panel). Its sole purpose is to mechanically disengage the parking pawl via a plunger when the driver presses the brake pedal and the key is in the "Run" position. If you hear a click but remain locked, the solenoid is likely receiving a momentary pulse but failing to maintain the latch or has a mechanical obstruction preventing the plunger from extending.

Regarding the doors not auto-unlocking upon shifting into Park, this is frequently a symptom of the same underlying issue rather than a separate fault. The logic flow in many GM platforms of this era ties the "Park" status signal directly to the door unlock command. When the BCM detects that the car is still mechanically locked in Park (due to the interlock failure), it may delay or skip the auto-unlock sequence as a safety measure, fearing the vehicle might roll if doors open while the parking brake is not fully engaged by the pawl. The unusual delay you observed suggests the system is trying to re-evaluate the gear status before commanding the unlock relay.

Since your 2007 Cobalt lacks an aftermarket-friendly shift interlock override (a small hole in the steering column shroud often found on later models), testing requires a multimeter or jumper wire approach. You can verify if the solenoid is receiving voltage by probing the connector while pressing the brake and shifting to Park. If you measure 12V at the coil terminals but hear no actuation (or only the initial click without movement), the solenoid is electrically functional for a split second but mechanically seized or internally shorted. If there is no voltage, the fault lies in the BCM logic or wiring harness leading to the column.

Replacing the shift interlock solenoid on this platform is generally considered user-serviceable. The part is located behind the trim panel near the steering column, typically requiring the removal of a few screws and the dashboard side panel. Be prepared to work in tight spaces where your knee may obstruct access. Ensure you disconnect the negative battery cable before working near any electrical connectors to prevent accidental shorts while manipulating the wiring harness.

If the replacement solenoid does not resolve the issue, the problem could be a failing brake switch sending an incomplete signal to the ECM, or a cracked wire in the steering column harness causing intermittent connection loss. Given the age of the vehicle and the low trade-in value, investing in these components is a valid strategy if you wish to extend its life, but be prepared for the possibility that the BCM itself has degraded reliability common in vehicles of this vintage.
